### Question 1

Sympathy stands at the top of a hole and calls down, 'that looks awful down there.' Empathy climbs partway in and says, 'I can see why it feels dark from where you are.' The climbing-partway part matters twice over: you have to get close enough to see it from their angle, and you have to say what you see out loud. Understanding someone silently does nothing for them, because they cannot tell the difference between being understood and being ignored.

### Question 2

Reflection mirrors feelings, not facts. People often say the feeling sideways: they describe what happened but never label how it landed. When you hand the emotion back to them in words, they get to look at it from the outside, which is much easier than examining it from inside. Sometimes they accept the label, sometimes they trade it for a better one, and either result moves the conversation forward.

### Question 3

Someone gives you directions and mumbles the street name. Guess, and you may drive twenty minutes the wrong way while feeling confident the whole time. Asking 'was that Maple or Marble?' costs five seconds. The phrasing matters too: 'I want to be sure I followed that' keeps the fault with you, while 'you're not being clear' puts the person on the defensive and makes the next answer shorter.

### Question 4

A lifeguard has to understand exactly how frightened a struggling swimmer is, otherwise the rescue is mistimed. What the lifeguard cannot do is start drowning alongside them, because then there are two people in the water and nobody on the board. Empathy is understanding the water while keeping your footing. Sympathy is getting pulled in, and it feels caring in the moment while leaving you less able to help.

### Question 5

Treat the feeling word as a draft, not a verdict. Declare 'you're angry' and a person who is actually humiliated has to argue with you before they can talk about anything else. Offer 'it sounds like maybe anger?' and they can simply say 'more like embarrassed,' which hands you the accurate word for free. Tentativeness is not hedging or weakness; it is the mechanism that lets the other person edit you.

### Question 6

Copy a drawing, then copy your copy, then copy that one. Three rounds later it barely resembles the original, and no single step felt wrong while you were doing it. Every guess you never check becomes the baseline for the next guess. Clarifying is going back to the original before you draw again, and the reason it falls to you is that patients rarely interrupt a professional to say 'that isn't what I meant.'

### Question 7

Validation says 'no wonder that hit you hard,' not 'you're right about what happened.' Those come apart cleanly: a person can be mistaken about a detail and still have a completely reasonable reaction to what they thought was true. Notice what the wrong moves do. 'You'll feel better soon' translates as 'stop feeling that,' and 'why do you feel that way?' translates as 'defend it first.' Both make the person work harder to be believed.

### Question 8

Fuzzy quantifiers carry a different meaning for every speaker. 'I drink socially' might mean two glasses a month or six on a Friday, and 'when things are normal' might mean most days or the rare calm week. Asking the person to describe what their own word looks like in practice turns a label into observable detail, and asking it in their words rather than yours avoids implying they answered badly.

### Question 9

Two moves in one sentence. First say what you heard beneath the words: nodding along to congratulations you do not feel is tiring. Then say that the reaction fits: of course you just nod, arguing would cost more energy than it is worth. Telling the person how lucky they are does the opposite; it hands them the same line they have been swallowing all week and asks them to swallow it once more.

### Question 10

Track where each sentence points. 'I feel terrible' points back at the speaker. 'That poor family' points down at the person. 'The same thing happened to me' points at the speaker's past. Only 'you're carrying a lot, and the waiting seems hardest' points at the other person and stays there long enough for them to answer. A useful test: could they reply 'actually, it's the nights that are worst'? If your sentence leaves room for that correction, it is doing empathic work.

### Question 11

Two sentences, two subjects. 'It makes complete sense that you're sick of being managed' is about how they feel. 'I don't think this plan is safe, and here's why' is about what they intend to do. Saying the first does not commit you to the second, and skipping the first rarely buys you anything, because a person who feels dismissed spends the conversation defending their autonomy instead of examining the plan.

### Question 12

Think of it as diagnose, confirm, then reassure. Find out what actually happened before you name a feeling about it, because 'you must be furious with your sister' lands badly if the sister was the one helping. Once the content is straight, say the feeling back so it can be corrected. Only then does 'no wonder that shook you' mean anything, because now you are agreeing about the right event.
